question:
Which of the following idioms given in the alternatives has the meaning?

"To reveal information unintentionally, especially about a plan that was to be kept secret."
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. To spill the beans.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "to spill the beans" means to disclose a secret, usually by accident or prematurely. (भेद खोल देना / राज़ उगल देना)
◦ Example: He spilled the beans about the transfer before the order was issued.

 

• The expression is generally traced to an ancient Greek voting practice, in which white and black beans were dropped into a jar; if the jar was upset before the count, the result was revealed too soon.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "To spill over the edge", Option 3: "To spill milk over" and Option 4: "To take the spill" are not established English idioms. Each has been formed by altering the wording of the genuine expression, and none of them carries any accepted meaning.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the genuine idiom "to cry over spilt milk", which means to waste time regretting something that cannot now be undone. It should not be confused with "to spill milk over", which is not an idiom at all.

 

• Related idioms about disclosure: "To let the cat out of the bag", "To blow the whistle on" (to expose wrongdoing), "To give the game away" and, on the other side, "To keep something under one's hat".

question:
From the alternatives given below, select the correct meaning of the idiom.

"A blessing in disguise."
option_1: A gift given secretly to avoid attention
option_2: A person who conceals his true intentions
option_3: A promise that is never intended to be kept
option_4: A misfortune that eventually turns out to be advantageous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A misfortune that eventually turns out to be advantageous.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The idiom "a blessing in disguise" means something that appears at first to be a misfortune, but which later proves to be of benefit. (छिपा हुआ वरदान)
◦ Example: Losing that job proved to be a blessing in disguise, for it led him to start his own business.

 

• The force of the idiom lies in the word "disguise" — the advantage is not recognised at the time, and becomes apparent only afterwards.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 describes anonymous giving, for which one might say "to do good by stealth".

 

• Option 2 describes a deceitful person — "a wolf in sheep's clothing" or "to wear a mask".

 

• Option 3 describes an empty promise — "to promise the moon" or "a pie-crust promise".

 

NOTE

 

• Related idioms about unexpected good fortune: "Every cloud has a silver lining", "To turn the tables", "A windfall" and "When one door closes, another opens".

 

• The opposite idea — an apparent gain that proves harmful — is conveyed by "a Greek gift", "a poisoned chalice" and "a white elephant".

question: Choose the correctly spelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Committee.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct spelling is "Committee" — a group of persons appointed to consider or manage some matter. (समिति)
◦ Example: The committee submitted its report to the Speaker last week.

 

• Spelling key: the word has three pairs of double letters — double "m", double "t" and double "e" — COM-MIT-TEE. Remembering "two of everything after CO" makes it easy.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "Comittee" — incorrect; only one "m" has been used.

 

• Option 3: "Commitee" — incorrect; only one "t" has been used.

 

• Option 4: "Committe" — incorrect; only one "e" has been used at the end.

 

NOTE

 

• Note the related forms, which do not double the "t" in the same way: commit, commitment (single "t"), but committed, committing, committee (double "t"). The rule is that the final consonant of *commit* is doubled before a suffix beginning with a vowel.

 

• Other words with multiple double letters: accommodation, possession, embarrass, Mississippi, aggressive and millennium.

question:
Select the option with the correct spelling that can replace the underlined word in the given sentence. If the spelling in the given sentence is already correct, choose Option 4 "No replacement required".

The lawyer presented an irrefutible argument that convinced the entire bench.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. irrefutable.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The word in the sentence, "irrefutible", is misspelt. The correct spelling is "irrefutable", ending in "-able", not "-ible". (अकाट्य / अखंडनीय)

 

• "Irrefutable" means impossible to deny or disprove.
◦ Example: The prosecution produced irrefutable evidence of the forgery.

 

• The corrected sentence reads: *The lawyer presented an irrefutable argument that convinced the entire bench.*

 

• A useful guide: when the root is a complete English word — *refute* — the suffix is usually "-able" (refute → refutable → irrefutable). When the root is not a complete word, the suffix is often "-ible" (*audible, visible, terrible*).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "iriffutable" — incorrect; the prefix "ir-" has been wrongly doubled into "irif".

 

• Option 3: "irrefutabel" — incorrect; the final letters "le" have been transposed.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect because the given word is misspelt and does require replacement.

 

NOTE

 

• Words taking "-able": *refutable, comfortable, reliable, acceptable, remarkable, inevitable, indispensable.*

 

• Words taking "-ible": *audible, visible, terrible, edible, legible, plausible, feasible, eligible, responsible.*

 

• Note the prefix "ir-", used before roots beginning with r — *irregular, irrelevant, irrational, irresistible, irreversible*.

question:
There are four underlined words in the sentence given below. One of them is misspelt. Choose the option with the misspelt word.

The audit revealed serious discrepencies in the accounts, the *inventory* records and the annual *statements*.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. discrepencies.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "discrepencies". The correct spelling is "discrepancies", with an "a" before the ending. (विसंगतियाँ / असंगतियाँ)

 

• "Discrepancy" means a difference between two things that ought to agree; an inconsistency. Its plural is formed by changing the "y" to "ies" — *discrepancy → discrepancies*.
◦ Example: The auditor pointed out several discrepancies between the vouchers and the ledger.

 

• The corrected sentence reads: *The audit revealed serious discrepancies in the accounts, the inventory records and the annual statements.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "accounts" — correctly spelt.

 

• Option 3: "inventory" — correctly spelt; note the ending "-ory".

 

• Option 4: "statements" — correctly spelt.

 

NOTE

 

• The related adjective is discrepant, which explains the "a" in *discrepancy* — adjectives in "-ant" give nouns in "-ancy/-ance", and those in "-ent" give nouns in "-ency/-ence".
◦ *discrepant → discrepancy*; *vacant → vacancy*; *relevant → relevance*
◦ *urgent → urgency*; *consistent → consistency*; *different → difference*

 

• Rule for plurals: a noun ending in consonant + y changes the y to -ies — *discrepancy → discrepancies, city → cities, army → armies*. A noun ending in vowel + y simply adds -s — *key → keys, day → days*.

question: Choose the misspelt word from the given options.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Turbulance.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The misspelt word is "Turbulance". The correct spelling is "Turbulence", ending in "-ence". (अशांति / विक्षोभ)
◦ Example: The aircraft passed through severe turbulence over the mountains.

 

• The rule that decides it: the adjective is "turbulent", ending in "-ent", and adjectives in "-ent" form nouns in "-ence". Had the adjective been "turbulant", the noun would have taken "-ance".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "Prevalence" — correctly spelt; from the adjective prevalent.

 

• Option 3: "Reluctance" — correctly spelt; from the adjective reluctant.

 

• Option 4: "Coincidence" — correctly spelt; from the adjective coincident.

 

NOTE

 

• Nouns in "-ence" (from adjectives in "-ent"): *turbulence, prevalence, competence, excellence, existence, independence, obedience, persistence, coincidence, patience.*

 

• Nouns in "-ance" (from adjectives in "-ant"): *reluctance, brilliance, relevance, tolerance, importance, resistance, assistance, appearance, maintenance.*

 

• The single most reliable way to settle such questions in the examination hall is to recall the adjective first, and then apply the -ant/-ance and -ent/-ence rule.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of "concealed".
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Exposed.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Concealed" means kept out of sight; hidden or covered up. (छिपाया हुआ)
◦ Example: The weapon was concealed under a heap of straw.

 

• "Exposed" means uncovered, laid open to view or made known, and is therefore the correct antonym. (उजागर / अनावृत)
◦ Example: The inquiry exposed a long-standing racket in the department.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Hidden (छिपा हुआ): Put or kept out of sight — a synonym of concealed, not an antonym.

 

• Option 2: Disguised (प्रच्छन्न): Given a false appearance so as not to be recognised — again close in sense.

 

• Option 4: Covered (ढका हुआ): Placed under a covering — also a synonym in this context.

 

NOTE

 

• Synonyms of concealed: Secreted, Veiled, Camouflaged, Obscured, Cloaked.

 

• Synonyms of exposed: Revealed, Unveiled, Uncovered, Divulged, Disclosed, Laid bare.

 

• Note the related noun "concealment" and the legal phrase "concealment of facts", which is frequently used in official English.

question: Choose the word that is the antonym of "Ascending".
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Descending.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Ascending" means going or moving upward; rising. (आरोही / ऊपर चढ़ता हुआ)
◦ Example: The names were arranged in ascending order of seniority.

 

• "Descending" means going or moving downward, and is therefore the correct antonym. (अवरोही / नीचे उतरता हुआ)
◦ Example: The marks were listed in descending order, the highest first.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: Climbing (चढ़ना): Moving upward, especially with effort — a synonym of ascending.

 

• Option 3: Rising (उठता हुआ): Moving to a higher position — again a synonym.

 

• Option 4: Soaring (ऊँचा उड़ना): Rising high and rapidly, as a bird or a price — also close in sense.

 

NOTE

 

• The pair is worth remembering in its mathematical sense as well: numbers arranged from smallest to largest are in ascending order, and from largest to smallest in descending order.

 

• Related pairs: ascent - descent, ascend - descend, upward - downward, uphill - downhill and elevate - lower.

question:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

The government took prompt steps to ______ the disturbance before it could spread.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. quell.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Quell" is a verb meaning to put an end to a rebellion or disturbance, usually by force; to suppress. (दबाना / शांत करना)
◦ Example: The police were called in to quell the riot.

 

• The completed sentence reads: *The government took prompt steps to quell the disturbance before it could spread.*

 

• The four options form a set of similar-sounding words with entirely different meanings, and only "quell" fits the sense of putting down a disturbance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "quail" (भयभीत होना): As a verb it means to lose courage or shrink with fear — *He did not quail before the threat.* As a noun it is a small game bird. It cannot take an object such as "the disturbance".

 

• Option 3: "quill" (पंख / कलम): A large feather, or a pen made from one; also the sharp spine of a porcupine.

 

• Option 4: "quilt" (रजाई): A thick padded bed covering.

 

NOTE

 

• "Quell" is also used of feelings — *to quell one's anxiety*, meaning to calm or subdue it.

 

• Other near-homophone sets frequently tested: canvas/canvass, dessert/desert, envelop/envelope, elicit/illicit, allusion/illusion, prescribe/proscribe and council/counsel.

question:
Choose the correct word to complete the sentence.

Migratory birds must ______ themselves to the harsh conditions of the desert.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. adapt.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Adapt" is a verb meaning to adjust or become adjusted to new conditions. (अनुकूल बनाना / ढल जाना)
◦ Example: The plants have adapted themselves to a very dry climate.

 

• The completed sentence reads: *Migratory birds must adapt themselves to the harsh conditions of the desert.*

 

• The verb is often used reflexively — *adapt oneself to* — and takes the preposition "to".

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "adept" (निपुण): An adjective meaning highly skilled or proficient — *He is adept at handling difficult customers.* It is not a verb and cannot take "themselves".

 

• Option 2: "adopt" (अपनाना / गोद लेना): A verb meaning to take up a practice, or to take another's child legally as one's own — *The committee adopted the resolution.* It does not carry the sense of adjusting to conditions.

 

• Option 4: "addict" (व्यसनी बनाना): Chiefly a noun meaning a person dependent on a habit, and as a verb *to addict oneself to* something harmful.

 

NOTE

 

• The distinction is a favourite in SSC papers:
◦ Adapt — to adjust: *He adapted quickly to village life.*
◦ Adopt — to take up or take in: *India adopted its Constitution in 1949.*
◦ Adept — skilled: *She is adept in three languages.*

 

• The related nouns are adaptation (adjustment), adoption (taking up) and adeptness (skill).

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

The person who writes the words of a song or an opera.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Lyricist.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• A "lyricist" is a person who writes the words, or lyrics, of a song. (गीतकार) The words themselves are the lyrics, and in opera they are called the libretto, written by a librettist.
◦ Example: The film's success owed much to its lyricist, whose songs were on everyone's lips.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Composer (संगीतकार): A person who writes the music, as distinct from the words.

 

• Option 2: Vocalist (गायक): A singer, that is, one who performs the song rather than writes it.

 

• Option 3: Conductor (वादक-वृंद संचालक): A person who directs an orchestra or a choir, keeping the performers in time.

 

NOTE

 

• Other one-word substitutions for people in the arts:
◦ Choreographer — one who designs the steps of a dance
◦ Cinematographer — one who is in charge of the camera work of a film
◦ Playwright — one who writes plays (note the spelling: *wright*, a maker, not *write*)
◦ Scriptwriter / Screenwriter — one who writes screenplays
◦ Sculptor — one who carves in stone or wood
◦ Cartographer — one who draws maps
◦ Calligrapher — one skilled in beautiful handwriting
◦ Virtuoso — a person with outstanding technical skill in music

question:
Choose the most suitable one-word substitution for the following.

The study of the origin and history of words.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Etymology.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Etymology" is the study of the origin of words and of the way in which their meanings have changed through history. (शब्द-व्युत्पत्ति विज्ञान)
◦ Example: The etymology of the word "salary" takes us back to the Latin *salarium*, the money paid to Roman soldiers to buy salt.

 

• The word comes from the Greek *etymon*, meaning the true or original sense of a word.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: Philology (भाषाशास्त्र): The study of language, especially in written historical sources, and of the relationships between languages. It is broader than etymology, which is concerned specifically with the origins of individual words.

 

• Option 3: Entomology (कीटविज्ञान): The study of insects. The similarity of sound to *etymology* makes this the commonest trap in the question.

 

• Option 4: Lexicography (कोश-रचना): The practice of compiling dictionaries; one who does so is a lexicographer.

 

NOTE

 

• A quick way to keep the pair apart: Etymology contains "etym", related to *term* and *word*; Entomology contains "ent", as in *insect*.

 

• Other related terms: Semantics (the study of meaning), Phonetics (the study of speech sounds), Syntax (the arrangement of words), Morphology (the study of word forms) and Orthography (the study of spelling).

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition in the following sentence.

The meeting was postponed ______ short notice because of the strike.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. at.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The fixed expression is "at short notice", meaning with very little warning or time for preparation. (अल्प सूचना पर)
◦ Example: He was asked to leave for Delhi at short notice.

 

• The completed sentence reads: *The meeting was postponed at short notice because of the strike.*

 

• Note the related expressions, all of which take "at": *at any rate, at all costs, at a stretch, at large, at length, at random, at once, at present* and *at the outset*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2: "on" is used in "on notice" in a different sense — *to serve notice on someone* — and in "on account of", "on behalf of" and "on the whole".

 

• Option 3: "in" appears in "in due course", "in the long run" and "in advance". Note that "in advance" is a near opposite in sense to "at short notice".

 

• Option 4: "by" appears in "by chance", "by and large", "by all means" and "by no means".

 

NOTE

 

• American usage prefers "on short notice", but SSC follows British usage, in which "at short notice" is standard.

 

• Other fixed phrases beginning with "at": at par, at stake, at variance with, at loggerheads, at the eleventh hour, at daggers drawn and at one's wit's end.

question:
Select the correct alternative to fill in the blank with the correct preposition or prepositional phrase in the following sentence.

The scheme was withdrawn ______ strong opposition from the trade unions.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. in the face of.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The prepositional phrase "in the face of" means in spite of, or when confronted with, something difficult or hostile. (के बावजूद / का सामना करते हुए)
◦ Example: She showed great courage in the face of adversity.

 

• The completed sentence reads: *The scheme was withdrawn in the face of strong opposition from the trade unions.* The sense required is that of a decision taken when confronted by opposition, which only this phrase supplies.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1: "at the mercy of" (के रहमोकरम पर): Wholly in the power of somebody or something, and unable to resist — *The boat was at the mercy of the waves.* It suggests helplessness rather than confrontation.

 

• Option 3: "on the strength of" (के आधार पर): On the basis of, relying upon — *He was appointed on the strength of his experience.* The sense here is the reverse of what the sentence requires.

 

• Option 4: "in the grip of" (की चपेट में): Firmly held or afflicted by something — *The country was in the grip of a severe drought.*

 

NOTE

 

• Other prepositional phrases frequently tested in SSC: in lieu of (in place of), in the wake of (following), in the teeth of (in direct opposition to), at the behest of (at the request of), under the aegis of (under the protection of), by dint of (by means of), with a view to (with the intention of) and in the event of (if something happens).

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

Does the library issue books to visitors?
option_1: Are books issued to visitors by the library?
option_2: Is books issued to visitors by the library?
option_3: Have books been issued to visitors by the library?
option_4: Are books being issued to visitors by the library?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Are books issued to visitors by the library?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is an interrogative sentence in the Simple Present Tense, beginning with the auxiliary "Does".

 

• Rule — Simple Present, interrogative:
◦ Active: Do/Does + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Is/Am/Are + Object + V3 + by + Subject?

 

• Applying the rule: the object "books" becomes the subject; it is plural, so the auxiliary is "Are"; "issue" becomes the past participle "issued"; and "the library" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: *Are books issued to visitors by the library?*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is incorrect — "Is" is singular, whereas the new subject "books" is plural. This is a subject-verb agreement error.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — "Have been issued" is the passive of the Present Perfect Tense.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — "Are being issued" is the passive of the Present Continuous Tense, which would mean the issuing is going on at this moment.

 

NOTE

 

• Note that "Does" in the active sentence agrees with the singular subject *the library*, but the passive auxiliary must agree with the new subject *books*, which is plural. The shift from *Does* to *Are* is exactly what the question tests.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Passive Voice?

Why didn't the committee accept his resignation?
option_1: Why wasn't his resignation accepted by the committee?
option_2: Why weren't his resignation accepted by the committee?
option_3: Why didn't his resignation accepted by the committee?
option_4: Why isn't his resignation accepted by the committee?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Why wasn't his resignation accepted by the committee?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is a negative wh-interrogative in the Simple Past Tense (Why + didn't + subject + V1 + object?).

 

• Rule — Simple Past, negative wh-interrogative:
◦ Active: Wh-word + did + not + Subject + V1 + Object?
◦ Passive: Wh-word + was/were + not + Object + V3 + by + Subject?

 

• Applying the rule: the question word "Why" keeps its place; the object "his resignation" becomes the subject and is singular, so the auxiliary is "wasn't"; "accept" becomes the past participle "accepted"; and "the committee" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: *Why wasn't his resignation accepted by the committee?*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 is incorrect — "weren't" is plural, but the new subject "his resignation" is singular.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — "didn't ... accepted" is impossible; after "did" only the base form may follow, and the structure is not passive at all.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — "isn't accepted" is the passive of the Simple Present Tense.

 

NOTE

 

• In negative sentences the "not" stays with the auxiliary in both voices. The auxiliary "did" disappears in the passive and is replaced by was/were, since "did" is only the marker of the Simple Past in negative and interrogative sentences.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice?

The old records were being digitised by the staff throughout the summer.
option_1: The staff digitised the old records throughout the summer.
option_2: The staff digitise the old records throughout the summer.
option_3: The staff have digitised the old records throughout the summer.
option_4: The staff were digitising the old records throughout the summer.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. The staff were digitising the old records throughout the summer.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is in the Past Continuous Tense, passive voice (was/were being + V3).

 

• Rule — Past Continuous Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were being + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + was/were + V-ing + Object

 

• Applying the rule: the agent "the staff" becomes the subject; "were being digitised" becomes "were digitising", that is, the word "being" is dropped and the past participle changes to the present participle.
◦ Active: *The staff were digitising the old records throughout the summer.*

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is incorrect — "digitised" alone is the Simple Past Tense and loses the sense of an action in progress over a period.

 

• Option 2 is incorrect — "digitise" is the Simple Present Tense.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — "have digitised" is the Present Perfect Tense.

 

NOTE

 

• Only the continuous tenses use "being" in the passive, and it must be removed when converting back to the active:
◦ *The house is being built.* → *They are building the house.*
◦ *The house was being built.* → *They were building the house.*

 

• The phrase "throughout the summer" indicates a continuing action, which is a further confirmation that the continuous tense must be retained.

question:
Which of the following options is the most suitable conversion of the following sentence into Active Voice?

Which newspapers are subscribed to by your office?
option_1: Which newspapers did your office subscribe to?
option_2: Which newspapers does your office subscribe to?
option_3: Which newspapers is your office subscribed to?
option_4: Which newspapers has your office subscribed to?
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Which newspapers does your office subscribe to?

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The given sentence is a wh-interrogative in the Simple Present Tense, passive voice (Which + object + are + V3 + by + agent?).

 

• Rule — Simple Present, wh-interrogative:
◦ Passive: Wh-word + is/are + Object + V3 + by + Subject?
◦ Active: Wh-word + do/does + Subject + V1 + Object?

 

• Applying the rule: the agent "your office" becomes the subject; it is singular, so the auxiliary is "does"; and "subscribed" reverts to the base form "subscribe", since only V1 may follow "does".
◦ Active: *Which newspapers does your office subscribe to?*

 

• Note that the preposition "to" belongs to the verb *subscribe to* and is retained in both voices.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 is incorrect — "did ... subscribe" is the Simple Past Tense.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — it remains passive in form and also uses a singular auxiliary with a plural subject.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — "has ... subscribed" is the Present Perfect Tense.

 

NOTE

 

• When a prepositional verb — *subscribe to, look after, deal with, laugh at, listen to* — is used in the passive, the preposition is not dropped:
◦ *They laughed at him.* → *He was laughed at.*
◦ *The nurse looked after the patient.* → *The patient was looked after by the nurse.*

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. A language is far more than a means of exchanging information.

A. When such a language dies, therefore, a whole way of describing the world dies with it.

B. Every language carries within it a particular way of dividing up experience.

C. Some have a dozen words for kinds of snow, others none at all.

D. The distinctions a community finds worth making are the distinctions its speech preserves.

S2. That is why the loss of a small tongue is a loss to everyone, and not merely to those who spoke it.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. BCDA.

• The correct sequence is S1 – B – C – D – A – S2, moving from a general claim → an example → the principle behind it → the consequence.

• B → C: C provides the illustration — some languages have a dozen words for kinds of snow, others none. An example must follow the general statement it illustrates.

 

• C → D: D draws out the principle underlying the example: the distinctions a community finds worth making are the ones its speech preserves.

 

• D → A: A begins with "When such a language dies, therefore". The word "therefore" marks a conclusion, and "such a language" refers back to the kind of language described in B, C and D.

 

• A → S2: S2 explains why that loss matters to everyone, following naturally from A.

Additional Information

 

• Option 2 (CBDA) is incorrect because C is an example and cannot precede the general statement in B that it illustrates.

 

• Option 3 (BDCA) is incorrect because it places the principle (D) before the example (C) that leads to it, which reverses the natural movement of the argument.

 

• Option 4 (DBCA) is incorrect because D is a conclusion drawn from B and C, and cannot come first among them.

 

NOTE

 

• A dependable order in expository paragraphs is general statement → example → principle → consequence. Sentences containing "therefore", "thus", "hence" or "that is why" almost always come late in the sequence.

question:
Given below are six sentences taken from a paragraph. The first and the last sentences are numbered S1 and S2 and are placed in the first and last positions respectively and are fixed in their positions. The other four sentences between the first and last sentences are jumbled up and are numbered A, B, C, and D. Rearrange the jumbled sentences in a logical sequence keeping the unity and coherence of the paragraph intact. Choose the correct alternative that best describes the sequence.

S1. At last the driver admitted that he had lost his way.

A. He had been driving for nearly two hours through the same flat country.

B. He stopped the jeep, switched off the engine and studied the sky for a while.

C. Away to the left a faint line of hills showed against the last of the light.

D. That, he said, must be the ridge above the village, and the road must lie beneath it.

S2. He turned the jeep towards the hills, and within twenty minutes we saw the first lamps of Rampur.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. ABCD.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The correct sequence is S1 – A – B – C – D – S2, moving from the situation → the halt → what he saw → what he concluded.

 

• S1 → A: S1 states that the driver admitted he had lost his way. A explains the background — he had been driving for nearly two hours through the same flat country, which is why he had become lost.

 

• A → B: B describes his action on admitting it — he stopped the jeep, switched off the engine and studied the sky.

 

• B → C: C records what he saw as a result of looking about him — a faint line of hills to the left. Observation must follow the act of looking.

 

• C → D: D gives his inference from that observation: *"That, he said, must be the ridge above the village."* The demonstrative "That" points directly back to the hills of C, which makes C-D a mandatory pair.

 

• D → S2: S2 records the action taken on that inference — he turned the jeep towards the hills — and its result.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 (BACD) is incorrect because the explanation of how he came to be lost (A) should follow S1 immediately, before he halts the vehicle.

 

• Option 3 (ABDC) is incorrect because D begins with "That", which must refer to the hills described in C; placing D before C leaves the demonstrative unanchored.

 

• Option 4 (BCAD) is incorrect because it strands A, the background explanation, in the middle of the sequence of actions.

 

NOTE

 

• Demonstratives — this, that, these, those, such — behave exactly like pronouns in para-jumbles: the sentence containing them must follow the sentence that supplies what they point to.

question:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the question based on the passage.

 

The early history of the Indian press is particularly well suited to a study of how public opinion was first formed, because the newspapers of that period were small, personal and almost wholly unsubsidised. Their limitations are obvious enough. Circulations were tiny, often a few hundred copies; the language of the principal journals was English, which shut out the great majority of readers; and the editors were drawn from a narrow professional class, so that the concerns of the countryside seldom found a place in their columns. Such papers were also intensely local, appearing and disappearing within a few years, and the same reader might in a decade see three or four journals rise and fail in his own town.
All this makes it difficult to accept without qualification the notion of an early 'national press'. The initiative and the courage of these editors were undoubted, and at times remarkable; but unlike the organised political journalism of a later generation, which possessed a continuity of argument running from the economic critique of the 1870s onward, the earlier papers were scattered and episodic. Each fought its own battle, and each was forgotten when its editor tired or its funds ran out.
Yet for all these limitations the early press anticipated much of what came afterwards. The questions it raised — the cost of administration, the working of the courts, the condition of tenants, the treatment of Indians in public service — were precisely the questions that a later and better organised journalism would take up and press home. Its achievements, if modest, were not negligible: it established the habit of public criticism, and that habit long outlived the papers themselves.

 

Why does the author consider the early Indian press particularly well suited to a study of how public opinion was formed?
option_1: Because its newspapers had very large circulations
option_2: Because its newspapers were small, personal and almost wholly unsubsidised
option_3: Because it was closely supervised by the colonial government
option_4: Because its editors were drawn from every class of society
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Because its newspapers were small, personal and almost wholly unsubsidised.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The passage states the reason in its very first sentence: *"The early history of the Indian press is particularly well suited to a study of how public opinion was first formed, because the newspapers of that period were small, personal and almost wholly unsubsidised."*

 

• The point is that such papers reflected the individual convictions of their editors rather than the interests of any patron or party, and so show public opinion in its earliest and least organised form.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Option 1 contradicts the passage, which says circulations were tiny, often a few hundred copies.

 

• Option 3 is not stated; government supervision is nowhere mentioned as the reason for the period's suitability.

 

• Option 4 is the opposite of what the passage says — the editors were drawn from "a narrow professional class".

 

NOTE

 

• When a question asks why the author holds a view, the answer is usually in the clause introduced by "because", "since", "as" or "for" in the opening sentence. Reading only the first sentence carefully will often settle such questions.

question: निम्नलिखित में से करेंसी नोटों का कौन-सा मूल्यवर्ग भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक द्वारा नहीं, बल्कि भारत सरकार द्वारा जारी किया जाता है?
solution_text:
सही उत्तर एक रुपये का नोट है।

महत्वपूर्ण बिंदु

• एक रुपये का नोट भारत सरकार द्वारा जारी किया जाता है, भारतीय रिज़र्व बैंक द्वारा नहीं। इस पर वित्त सचिव (Finance Secretary) के हस्ताक्षर होते हैं, जबकि शेष सभी नोटों पर RBI के गवर्नर के हस्ताक्षर होते हैं। (एक रुपये का नोट — भारत सरकार द्वारा जारी)

• सभी सिक्के तथा एक रुपये का नोट भारत सरकार द्वारा सिक्का निर्माण अधिनियम, 2011 (Coinage Act, 2011) के अंतर्गत जारी किए जाते हैं, जबकि दो रुपये और उससे अधिक मूल्यवर्ग के करेंसी नोट RBI द्वारा RBI अधिनियम, 1934 की धारा 22 के अंतर्गत जारी किए जाते हैं।

• एक रुपये का नोट सर्वप्रथम 1917 में जारी हुआ, 1994 में बंद कर दिया गया, और 2015 में पुनः आरंभ किया गया।

• RBI न्यूनतम आरक्षित प्रणाली (Minimum Reserve System) के अंतर्गत नोट जारी करता है, जिसके अनुसार उसे कम से कम ₹200 करोड़ की परिसंपत्तियाँ रखनी होती हैं, जिनमें से ₹115 करोड़ स्वर्ण में तथा ₹85 करोड़ विदेशी प्रतिभूतियों में होनी चाहिए। यह प्रणाली 1957 में आनुपातिक आरक्षित प्रणाली के स्थान पर अपनाई गई।

अतः सही उत्तर विकल्प 1 है।

अतिरिक्त जानकारी

• बैंक नोटों की महात्मा गांधी शृंखला 1996 में तथा महात्मा गांधी (नई) शृंखला 2016 में आरंभ हुई। करेंसी नोटों की छपाई नासिक, देवास, मैसूरु और सालबोनी की प्रेसों में होती है, तथा सिक्कों की ढलाई मुंबई, कोलकाता, हैदराबाद और नोएडा में की जाती है।
